files.lesson.md: --- order: 27 unit: trig9 node: AC9M9M03 n4 uses: [AC9M9M03 n1, AC9M9M03 n2, AC9M8M06 n2] assumes: [AC9M9M03 n2, AC9M9M03 n3] connection: ramp-1-in-14 title: Ramp to a door summary: "A real problem needs more than one tool. Draw the triangle, say which parts you know, and choose between a scale, Pythagoras and trigonometry for each part." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "The front door is 0.45 m above the path. How long does the ramp need to be?" --- Wheelchair ramps up to 9 m long can be at most 1 in 14: 1 m up for every 14 m along the ground ([Queensland Health](https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0029/1477208/Ramps-to-the-house-and-slopes-in-the-garden-slides.pdf)). A door is 0.45 m above the path (made up for the task). How far from the door does the ramp have to start, how long is the ramp surface, and what angle is it? Have a guess how long it needs to run along the ground, and we'll come back to it at the end. ## Predict: how long along the ground ```step stage: predict insight: "Finding the run for 1 in 14 and a 0.45 m rise shows whether students multiply the rise by 14 or confuse the run with the ramp's length." check: type: predict q: "The ramp must rise 0.45 m at a gradient of 1 in 14. How far along the ground does it run?" options: - "6.3 m" - "0.03 m" - "14 m" - "4.5 m" actual: "6.3 m. For every 1 m up it goes 14 m along, so 0.45 m up goes 0.45 × 14 = 6.3 m along." ``` ## Run: choose the tool ```step stage: run insight: "Each part of the problem names its own tool: the gradient fixes the run, Pythagoras gives the ramp's length, and an inverse ratio gives the angle." check: { type: number, q: "How long is the run along the ground for a 0.45 m rise at 1 in 14? (metres)", answer: 6.3, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "0.45 × 14 = 6.3 m." } ``` Think about the triangle: the rise and run are the two shorter sides and the ramp surface is the hypotenuse. ## Investigate: three parts, three tools ```step stage: investigate insight: "Pythagoras gives a third side from two; the angle comes from an inverse ratio of two sides; the gradient is itself a ratio of rise to run." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Rise $0.45$ m, run $6.3$ m. How long is the ramp surface, to 2 decimal places?" answer: 6.32 tolerance: 0.02 explain: "√(0.45² + 6.3²) = √39.8925 = 6.316, about 6.32 m." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $0.45^2 + 6.3^2$? (2 decimal places)", answer: 39.89, tolerance: 0.02, explain: "0.2025 + 39.69 = 39.8925." } - check: type: question q: "Which tool gives the angle of the ramp from the rise and the run?" options: ["tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run)", "Pythagoras", "The scale factor", "Adding the rise and run"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Pythagoras gives the ramp's length, not an angle.", "The scale factor compares similar shapes.", "Adding doesn't give an angle."] explain: "Rise is opposite and run is adjacent, so the angle is tan⁻¹(0.45 ÷ 6.3)." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ali" text: "Ali finds the ramp's angle. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: ratio-is-angle explain: "Line 2: 1 in 14 is a ratio (rise ÷ run). The angle is tan⁻¹(1 ÷ 14) = 4.1°, not 14°." ``` ### Three parts ```worked \text{run} = 0.45 \times 14 = 6.3 :: The gradient: 14 along for every 1 up. \text{ramp} = \sqrt{0.45^2 + 6.3^2} \approx 6.32 :: Pythagoras: the ramp is the hypotenuse. \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{0.45}{6.3}\right) = 4.1° :: Rise is opposite, run is adjacent. ``` ### Which tool ### Find the mistake Read Ali's working. Which line turns the gradient into an angle wrongly? ## Modify: change the door ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing the rise reruns the same three tools and tests whether the ramp limits still apply." tasks: - hint: ["Rise × 14.", "0.3 × 14."] check: { type: number, q: "A different door is $0.3$ m above the path. How long is the run for a 1 in 14 ramp? (metres)", answer: 4.2, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "0.3 × 14 = 4.2 m." } - hint: ["The run is 6.3 m.", "Is the ramp surface longer than the run?"] check: { type: question, q: "A student finds the ramp surface is $6.1$ m for a $6.3$ m run. What is wrong?", options: ["The hypotenuse can't be shorter than a shorter side", "Nothing", "The run is too long", "The ramp is too steep"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The ramp surface is the hypotenuse, so it must be the longest side.", "The run is a leg, and legs can be long.", "Steepness isn't the issue here."], explain: "The hypotenuse is always longer than either shorter side. 6.1 < 6.3 means a mistake." } - hint: ["0.9 × 14.", "The limit applies up to 9 m."] check: { type: question, q: "A door is $0.9$ m up, so a 1 in 14 ramp needs a run of $12.6$ m. Is the 1 in 14 rule enough?", options: ["No: that rule is for ramps up to 9 m, so a longer ramp needs the standard's other rules", "Yes: 1 in 14 always works", "Yes: it is shorter than 14", "No: a 0.9 m door needs stairs"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The limit given is for ramps up to 9 m long.", "The length of the ramp, not the number 14, is the issue.", "The standard allows longer ramps with other rules."], explain: "The 1 in 14 figure is for ramps up to 9 m. Longer ramps are covered by other rules, such as flatter slopes and landings: check the standard." } ``` ### A lower door ### Longer than the run ### Too tall ## Practise: choose the tool ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing between the gradient, Pythagoras and trigonometry." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A ramp rises $0.5$ m at 1 in 14. How long is the run? (metres)" answer: 7 explain: "0.5 × 14 = 7." - check: type: question q: "You know the rise and the run and want the ramp's length. Which tool?" options: ["Pythagoras", "tan⁻¹", "A scale factor", "Gradient 1 in 14"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "tan⁻¹ gives an angle.", "A scale factor needs a similar shape.", "That gives the run from the rise."] explain: "Two shorter sides give the hypotenuse by Pythagoras." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Is the ramp surface a shorter side or the hypotenuse?", options: ["The hypotenuse", "A shorter side", "Neither", "Both"], answer: 0, explain: "It is across from the right angle." } - check: type: number q: "Review: tan⁻¹ of 1 is what angle?" answer: 45 tolerance: 0.5 explain: "tan 45° = 1." ``` ### The run ### The tool ### Review ## Make: the whole ramp ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the door: all three parts, written up, with a note on what the ramp's maker also needs to check." tasks: - hint: ["Gradient, then Pythagoras, then the angle.", "tan⁻¹(0.45 ÷ 6.3)."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The door is 0.45 m above the path and the ramp is 1 in 14. What angle does the ramp make with the ground? (1 decimal place. The door height is made up for the task.)" steps: - ["run $= 0.45 \\times 14 = 6.3$", "use the gradient"] - ["$\\tan\\theta = 0.45 \\div 6.3 = 0.0714$", "rise over run"] - ["$\\theta = \\tan^{-1}(0.0714) = 4.1°$", "use the inverse key"] answer: "4.1" answerLabel: "Angle (degrees)" tolerance: 0.1 feedback: - ["14", "1 in 14 is a ratio, not an angle."] - ["6.3", "That is the run. Find the angle."] criteria: - "I used the run from the gradient." - "I named rise as opposite and run as adjacent." - "I used the inverse key." explain: "tan⁻¹(0.0714) = 4.1°, the same as for any 1 in 14 ramp." - check: type: question q: "What else must a ramp's designer check that this triangle doesn't show?" options: ["Landings, handrails and the rules for longer or shorter ramps", "Only the angle", "Only the length", "Nothing: the triangle is the whole design"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "There's more than the angle.", "There's more than the length.", "A triangle is just the shape of the slope."] explain: "The standard also covers landings, handrails and other gradients: the triangle only gives the slope." ``` ### The angle ### What the triangle misses **Also used in** - **Building and surveying.** Roofs, stairs, drains and roads all have a slope, a length and an angle. - **Physics.** A slope turns a push into a part along it. - **Next lesson.** What stays and what changes when a shape is enlarged. ```teacher summary: Students combine a gradient, Pythagoras and an inverse ratio to design a ramp to a door (AC9M9M03, node 4). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 6 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can choose the right tool for each part of a problem. - I can combine a gradient, Pythagoras and trigonometry. - I can say what the triangle doesn't tell me. struggle: "Not knowing where to start. Ask: draw the triangle: which two sides do you know?" before: > Students need Find an angle and Similar triangles and scale. The one idea: draw the triangle, say what is known and wanted, then pick the tool. Sources: the 1 in 14 limit is for ramps up to 9 m (AS 1428.1, via the Queensland Health slides). The door heights are made up for the task. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check." - "Paper: the ramp angle in Make is worked on paper first." stuck: - see: A student says the angle is 14°. ask: Is 1 in 14 an angle or a ratio? fix: "A ratio: rise ÷ run. The angle is tan⁻¹ of it." stretch: Design a ramp for a 0.9 m door and say what else the standard asks for. support: A printed triangle with rise, run and ramp labelled. leads: | Continues AC9M9M03 node 4. Where it leads: Enlargement and scale in two and three dimensions. exit: q: "Rise 1, run 14: which tool gives the angle?" a: tan⁻¹(1 ÷ 14). explain: > Draw the triangle and mark what you know. The gradient gives a side, Pythagoras gives the third side, and an inverse ratio gives the angle. Then check the answer makes sense. ```

# Ali's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: ali
The gradient is 1 in 14, so rise ÷ run = 1 ÷ 14.
That means the angle is 14°.
So the ramp is 14° to the ground.
